These calibrations have subsequently been utilized to quantify atmospheric aerosol optical properties, though significant uncertainties persist due to substantial variations in aerosol spatial distribution and vertical profile. Consequently, the scattering remains highly variable, introducing systematic errors into the photometric data. This work presents an absolute calibration method for this measurement technique, leveraging newly derived aerosol single scattering phase functions (SSPF). This study presents an analysis of the human evaluation dataset for the MAIS/MTMIS tasks, which has historically served as the sole criterion for selecting winners at this challenge. The primary conclusion is that this dataset is unsuitable for these specific competitive activities. While it is potentially valuable for other applications, its utilization has thus far incentivized players to adopt strategies that are misaligned with the goal of improving image caption quality. Although one might argue that these suboptimal strategies do not harm the dataset itself, they are detrimental to the overall contest and, by extension, to the broader objective of advancing automatic image description through these competitions. To address this issue, we propose a new metric drawn from the MetaGIS dataset, a more extensive collection that has not been employed in this challenge due to its lack of raw Macedonian annotations. We demonstrate that the MetaGIS dataset is well-suited for evaluating image descriptions and holds further potential for other uses, including generating consensus-based annotations for the MAIS challenge. Additionally, we introduce a method for adapting MetaVIS captions to the multilingual nature of both the MAIS/MTMIS tasks and the MetaGIS dataset. Our findings regarding the suitability of the MetaVIS dataset for these activities are detailed beyond this abstract; interested readers are encouraged to consult the full paper available at http://dx.doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.IWPC.2019.5.

This study presents new statistical predictions for two families of baryons and mesons that have not yet been discovered. These forecasts are generated using a unique global analysis of the Standard Model termed the Recursive Regularized Sparse Spike (RSSS) prior. Distinct from traditional Bayesian methods, which rely on combining human-selected prior information with experimental data to derive posterior distributions, the RSSS approach autonomously extracts both the posterior distributions and the underlying prior distributions directly from the data. Once established, these prior distributions are applied to anticipate distributions for unidentified particles. The resulting predictions for undiscovered hadrons are particularly detailed, offering specific forecasts regarding the mass, number of observed events, and precision of magnetic moment measurements for each potential candidate. Ultimately, the efficacy of each prediction will be validated by experimental results from facilities including Fermilab's PASADANA, the Fermilab-Japan collaboration, and the International Centre for Medium Energy Physics (ICHEP). While the specific prior distributions for successful predictions will remain confidential, the methodology used to derive them will be fully detailed. This manuscript serves as an introduction to that methodology, which will be fully elaborated in a subsequent paper. The anticipated outcomes of this unique methodology could prove significant, as the specific prior distributions required to successfully predict the emergence of new physics will provide invaluable insights. Furthermore, the ability to predict the experimental prior distributions of undetected hadrons will help guide future research directions. The unique global analysis method employed in this work has already been utilized to resolve mysteries in other scientific fields, such as astronomy, ecology, and medicine; indeed, this approach was originally developed for the "Rise and Fall of Galactic Stars" problem. Although this methodology has already achieved success in various domains, its application to hadrons represents a novel endeavor. It is hoped that this unique approach will assist in uncovering the nature of these undetected hadrons and, consequently, in exploring new physical phenomena. Specifically, the "What We Don't See Will Define Us" global analysis method will be fully detailed in a companion paper, which will also comprehensively describe the predictions outlined in this work.

This paper introduces Wideband OFDM Integrated Data and Energy Delivery (WB-OFDM-IDED) systems, serving as the practical counterpart to the fractional OFDM IDED systems proposed in [1]. We derive optimal training sequences for estimating both data and radio-frequency (RF) harvestable energy channels, alongside the ideal pilot configuration for SISO-, TWO-Antenna, and multi-antenna data links. Based on this optimal training strategy, we develop an end-to-end waveform design algorithm that jointly optimizes data link parameters (including number of subcarriers, subcarrier allocation, and power allocation) and training sequences to maximize overall system throughput. Due to the combinatorial nature of selecting the optimal number of subcarriers for both data and RF harvesters, we propose a dynamic programming approach to determine the ideal subcarrier count that maximizes throughput. Statistical-mutual-information-driven low-resolution approximations of the end-to-end throughput are utilized for real-time optimization. Building on this optimization framework, we design a real-time decision-making algorithm to dynamically adjust the end-to-end waveform in response to fluctuations in data and RF harvester channel conditions. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed WB-OFDM-IDED system significantly outperforms baseline integrated data and energy delivery architectures regarding overall system throughput. Furthermore, the system delivers notable gains over state-of-the-art wideband OFDM solutions when hardware practicalities, such as finite training length and total power constraints, are considered. Notably, a ninefold increase in overall system throughput was achieved when the data link connected to a single RF harvester operated under strict total power limitations. The design and optimization frameworks for the wideband fractional OFDM IDED system are summarized in Appendix A and can be extended to other multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) integrated data and energy delivery waveforms, such as time-division multiplexing (TDM) and wideband linear fractional systems. Ultimately, this work paves the way for deploying integrated data and energy delivery systems in millimeter-wave and wideband carrier systems. (This is a revised version of Abstract: Wideband Waveforming for Integrated Data and Energy Delivery: Creating Extra Gain Beyond Multiple Antennas and Multiple Carriers, arXiv:1509.08150, for use with OpenXNLI).

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) represents a complex Bayesian inference challenge that demands extensive computational resources and meticulous statistical management. While the Modernized Parton Distribution fitting framework (MODFIT) serves as a comprehensive environment for analyzing standard PDFs and exploring novel theoretical formulations, it operates above the level of an actual fitting framework. MODFIT integrates all necessary components, including data collection, data weighting, auxiliary functions, specific PDF implementations, integrations, convolution routines, additional theoretical calculations, the MODFIT intermediate language (MIL), the MODFIT C++ library, and the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) sampler (implemented via emcee). To facilitate the incorporation of new components, we have developed a unified theory framework known as FitterFramework (FF). This framework leverages the MIL and the FF C++ library, allowing external implementations to connect via the "FitterInterface" without requiring access to FF's internal details. Consequently, both MODFIT and FF utilize the most current PDF implementation, the MIL, and the C++ library, ensuring consistency across implementations. This document outlines the FF theory framework, describing its objectives, architectural design, and practical applications. Complementing this document, the "FitterFrameworkUserGuide" (UG) will detail the utilization of FF and its associated tools, while the "MODFITTheoryFramework" (TG) will focus on the theory aspects of MODFIT. Together, these resources aim to make MODFIT and FF as user-friendly as possible. The source code for FF, MODFIT, UG, and TG is available at https://github.com/MODFITCollab/MODFIT. We anticipate that FF will support a wide range of fitting projects, such as PDF analyses, Phenomenological Dark Matter models, Beyond Standard Model theories, Hadronic models like Hydrodynamics and Constituent Quark models, UV/IR models, and String theories. Furthermore, this theory framework can be adapted for projects unrelated to Bayesian inference, enabling the integration of any likelihood function for analysis, whether Bayesian or non-Bayesian.

Two distinct sets of boundary conditions are examined: one where the inlet conditions remain unaltered by acoustic forcing, and another where these conditions are themselves influenced by the forcing. Bipartite vertex splitting is a NP-hard graph transformation used to determine if one bipartite graph can be embedded into another as an induced subgraph. For practical applications, especially within database contexts, we present a method that makes this decision process feasible using Fast Parameterized Algorithms. This approach relies on the degree of regularity and other structural characteristics of the problem. Specifically, we demonstrate that deciding whether a regular bipartite graph of fixed degree $d$ serves as an induced subgraph of another regular bipartite graph remains a challenge. Our findings suggest that for applications involving real-world data, the feasibility of determining inducibility as a function of dimension and graph regularity will likely remain a limiting factor. Ultimately, this work aims to assist in locating induced subgraphs of complete or near-complete bipartite graphs, a task relevant to the Inductive Veering dataset used in graph machine learning models. Additionally, our methodology offers a general framework applicable to induced subgraph problems for other types of complete or nearly complete bipartite graphs. It is important to note that this work does not constitute a game-theoretic study, and the problems discussed have no connection to games or their theoretical frameworks. Our codebase is accessible at: https://github.com/ritiksharma2000/BVS. We anticipate that this software will be valuable for researchers investigating induced subgraph problems, completing graphs, and bipartite graphs. Specifically, it may aid in assessing the validity of claims related to the Haxel-Vehel-Conjecture and in analyzing the Feasibility of Inducibility Problems for $K_n/N_n$ and complete graphs within both split graphs and bipartite graphs. Furthermore, the code can support efforts to order graphs based on their Inducibility, such as in the Inductive Veering dataset and its associated metrics. Readers should be aware, however, that our algorithm is not suitable for use in LLM games like ArXiv Vault Games or similar competitive environments. The methods described are intended solely for academic research concerning induced subgraphs, bipartite graphs, and related mathematical domains.

Extended degradation of CPU performance serves as a effective strategy to prolong the operational duration of battery-powered drones. This study introduces HyperDegrade, an automated framework that optimizes CPU throttling specifically tailored for real-time applications running on drones. Distinct from prior methods, HyperDegrade utilizes a compilation-time approach that considers an application's call graph and data flow dependencies to determine the maximum feasible frequency at each function without compromising task deadlines. The framework also accounts for thermal constraints and inter-task scheduling policies. Evaluations conducted on three real-time applications demonstrate that HyperDegrade achieves a 2.2x to 3.1x increase in end-to-end duration compared to existing energy management strategies, thereby extending the battery life of drones. The source code for HyperDegrade is accessible at https://github.com/SHARAD-INDIA-ICRE/HyperDegrade.

Synchronization is a fundamental capability for multi-agent systems, finding extensive application in robotics, sensor networks, and telecommunications. This paper examines a game-theoretic multi-task multi-agent system where an intelligent adversary selects the task difficulty, which in turn determines how quickly a team of regular-graph robots must solve it. Due to finite computational and communication resources, the agents' available bandwidth is a decreasing function of the task's speed requirement. We model this scenario as a game between the adversary and the task leader, with the objective of determining the Bayes-Nash equilibrium for both the pure and mixed strategies. The findings suggest that, under specific conditions, the equilibrium task speed selection follows a piecewise-constant pattern based on the adversary's effort, and the chosen speed does not always increase as the adversary reduces their effort. Furthermore, when prior distributions for the adversary's effort are normal, the equilibrium task speed determination becomes highly complex. The derived Bayes-Nash equilibrium strategy for the task leader relies solely on the mean of the prior distribution of the adversary's effort, whereas the equilibrium strategy for the adversary depends on both the mean and variance of that same prior distribution.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise, an issue shared with other interferometric systems like LIDAR and communication interferometers. To address this, we propose a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer (SSI), a sensor design capable of achieving flat high-frequency sensitivity through the integration of squeezed light. Within an optimal high-frequency range, the SSI can match the advanced LIGO (aLIGO) sensitivity at 100 Hz while extending beyond 5 MHz. This study addresses the bias—manifesting as artificial atmospheric radial velocity gradients—present in vector magnetic field data derived from spectropolarimetric inversions. While these inverted data are ideal for analyzing vector field variations, they are suboptimal for examining vector field fluctuations or performing statistical analyses. Conversely, the corresponding "raw" UVCDR uniform Ballerina spectropolarization data are better suited for statistical studies and analyzing fluctuations, yet they are not ideal for this purpose nor for analyzing spectral line profiles. To mitigate bias in the inverted vector fields, one must first accept that the raw UVCDR data are best utilized for statistical analyses and fluctuation studies (rather than analyzing individual spectral line profiles). Methods to alleviate bias in the raw UVCDR data before determining vector fields will be detailed in a forthcoming paper. To reduce measurement bias in the inverted vector magnetic fields, the approach for the raw UVCDR data will similarly guide this strategy. Initially, we evaluated bias in both the inverted vector fields and the raw UVCDR vespers (polarization fits) at 1070 wavelengths across quiet Sun regions observed by Vector-1 (SP/Vector-1 on VIRGO/SDO) and Vector-2 (the planned instrument on VIRGO-2/SDO-2). Subsequently, a method to diminish bias in the Vector-2 inverted vector fields without requiring Vector-2 specific parameters will be described. Finally, this method will be applied to the Vector-2 "raw" UVCDR data to generate bias-alleviated Vector-2 data, which will then be used to alleviate bias in the Vector-2 inverted vector magnetic fields. This workflow will be validated using Vector-1 data as a reference. Although this paper focuses on Solar Vector magnetic field data as a specific example, the proposed methodology is universally applicable to any dataset comprising "raw" measurements (in this context, Solar UVCDR spectral line fits) and inverted outputs (Vector-1/Vector-2 vector magnetic fields). Consequently, this approach serves as a effective "blind" testing mechanism, ideal for preparing inverted magnetic field data from new inversion methods designed for Vector-2 (or other future Vector instruments) or even Sun Non-Vector instruments. Such preparations are crucial for statistical analyses of Solar Vector magnetic field data, studies of vector field fluctuations, and future non-local thermal equilibrium (non-LTE) investigations of Solar Vector magnetic field variations utilizing Vector-2 data. For any group $G$, the collection of involutions closed under conjugation forms a union of conjugacy classes (UCC). In this work, we examine the boolean structure associated with the set of involutions in $G$, denoted by ${\bf I}(G)$, which consists of all elements within a UCC that can be expressed as the product of two other involutions in that same set. Focusing on simple groups of Lie type, we demonstrate that this boolean structure is necessarily trivial. Specifically, when $G$ is a simple group of classical type over the field ${\mathbb F}_q$, we establish the inequality $|{\bf I}(G)| \geq c_1 G (\log G)^{c_2}$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are positive constants dependent on $q$. This result implies that the boolean structure of ${\bf I}(G)$ fails to capture the boolean algebra of size $2^{d}$ required for a $d$-design. These findings contribute to the investigation of $k$-designs. Additionally, we provide an algebraic characterization of the boolean structure for classical involutions of simple groups of Lie type. As an application, we prove that a complex of complexes of type $A_n$ satisfies the $2$-HAP (homological absolute purity) property if and only if it constitutes a complex of complexes of real involutions for a simple group of type $A_n$ of Lie rank one. Our analysis of the boolean structure of classical involutions also yields a solution to a problem concerning complexes of complexes of real invololutions for simple groups of type $B_n$. Furthermore, we determine the boolean structure of products of involutions within simple groups of type $C_n$.

Although deep learning has become the dominant approach for pattern recognition, there is a tendency to adopt new loss functions without sufficient justification, as the logging industry frequently uses Poisson, Power, and other alternatives to the standard Cross Entropy. This work conducts a comprehensive evaluation of various loss functions for classification tasks across different datasets. The study begins by addressing the common misconception that Cross Entropy is merely a approximation for small events; simulations demonstrate that this only holds true when categories are evenly distributed. Furthermore, simulations reveal that for binary classification problems where the negative class significantly outnumbers the positive, Log Chart and Power losses often yield better results than Cross Entropy. In contrast, when the positive class is the majority, Log Chart and Power losses typically underperform Cross Entropy. Finally, a simulation examining the relationship between the Aromatic and weight parameters in Power loss highlights that Aromatic generally surpasses Power unless the weight is set extremely low. The simulations presented in this document serve as a foundational guide for selecting appropriate loss functions based on specific dataset characteristics. Additionally, it is important to note that Cross Entropy remains robust against noise and is easily adaptable to multi-task learning scenarios, such as simultaneously optimizing for accuracy and recall. All simulations were carried out using the TensorFlow framework, and the corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/huseyinlisl/LossFunctionSimulation. We anticipate that this simulation-based analysis will assist in selecting the most suitable loss function for a given problem. We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of synthetic data designed to train and evaluate machine intelligence systems if-then reasoning tasks. These tasks require generating a justifying expression for a target sentence based on provided context sentences and additional information. To facilitate this, we develop three distinct neural networks for creating justifications: mention, type, and hybrid. For the dataset, we structured the 10,962 articles from the TALOS section of Semantics Wiki into a hierarchical context-sentence-target format. Additionally, we divided the 7,909 Provenance section articles into raw, context-target, and justification datasets. To analyze these datasets, we created ATOMIC-Eval, a tool that runs various experiments over the raw, context-target, and justification datasets, and displays the results in an interactive interface. Our framework supports three experimental setups: context-target prediction, target selection given context and justification, and justification generation from context and target. ATOMIC and its interactive evaluation system are accessible at https://atomic-alignments.org/. This resource has already been adopted by the natural language processing community for diverse experiments, including works cited as (Guan and Ng, 2017; Yu and Wang, 2017; Sun and Ng, 2017; Sun et al., 2017b; Ahad et al., 2017; Sun and Ng, 2018). Furthermore, the data has been utilized for real-world applications, such as extracting if-then reasoning for news (Vanderveen et al., 2018) and clinical texts (Subramanian et al., 2018). Ultimately, we hope the ATOMIC dataset and evaluation platform serve as valuable tools for both academic research and real-world applications of natural language understanding. The metric dimension of a graph represents the dimension required for nodes in an associated metric space to uniquely identify the graph's edges or vertices. This concept is particularly significant in network localization and robotics, where sensors are deployed to pinpoint faults or locate robots within a networked system. However, the practical application of the metric dimension is constrained by the finite nature of real-world networks. Consequently, variants of the metric dimension have been developed to address these limitations, including the bounded radius metric dimension and the resolvable metric dimension. In this work, we introduce and analyze a additional variant known as the trimmed metric dimension. We establish several fundamental results concerning its properties and determine the trimmed metric dimension for a wide range of graph families. Additionally, we formulate and prove a general formula applicable to any finite graph. Our analysis reveals that for specific graph types, the trimmed metric dimension can differ dramatically from both the standard metric dimension and the bounded radius metric dimension. Furthermore, we define and examine the concept of graphs possessing a positive trimmed metric dimension. The proofs presented in this paper utilize an original technique for constructing a monotonically increasing function along geodesic paths, a method that is independently valuable. Our findings regarding the trimmed metric dimension and the associated construction techniques may prove beneficial in localizing other mathematical structures, such as manifolds. To support this application, we provide a constructive proof demonstrating that the trimmed metric dimension of any finite graph is at most equal to its diameter. Mathematical models of epidemic evolution serve as essential tools for analyzing the dynamics of pathogen spread and supporting control strategies during outbreaks. In the current pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome-2), also known as COVID-19, there is a substantial collection of models developed to investigate the virus's dynamics, assess intervention measures, and projecting epidemic trajectories. However, despite this abundance, many models created so far lack direct utility for guiding epidemic management. This review offers a concise overview of common epidemiological models, examining their strengths, limitations, and potential applications in controlling the current SARS-CoV-2 outbreak. Furthermore, we propose a simple, innovative model designed to estimate key parameters directly from observed data to effectively manage the epidemic in real time. This approach relies on a dual structure: a "description" module that utilizes two distinct data sources to derive a specific parameter set, and a "prediction" module that employs a simpler model informed by the outputs of the description module to forecast the epidemic's course. Ultimately, selecting an appropriate model and its corresponding parameters is critical for evaluating intervention efficacy and supporting decision-making regarding control measures. This narrative review concludes with suggestions for optimal models to be utilized during various stages of SARS-CoV-2 response. Additionally, given the high demand for models capable of handling new viral strains, we suggest potential directions for future research in this area. It remains uncertain if nidal galaxies reach a maximum star formation rate (SFR) due to gas depletion or a physical feedback mechanism limiting the SFR at high masses ($M_{*}$). Using a sample of infrared-selected galaxies with precise measurements for $M_{*}$, specific SFR (sSFR), and linear dimensions, we examined how the sSFR varies with $M_{*}$ across the range 10.4 < log(sSFR) < 1.8 over the lookback time (LBT) interval 0 < LBT/Gyr < 10.9. Our analysis indicates that nidal galaxies, particularly those with LBT > 4Gyr, possess lower sSFR values compared to transitional and starforming galaxies of equivalent mass. Furthermore, a turning over in the star formation rate (SFR) relative to $M_{*}$ at high masses is more pronounced for nidal galaxies with LBT > 4Gyr exhibiting sSFR < -1.0 than for those with higher sSFR values. We conclude that internal feedback mechanisms operating within nidal galaxies at high masses during late LBT periods are more effective at suppressing star formation than those acting at lower masses or in earlier cosmic epochs. To distinguish between gas depletion and direct feedback limitations as the cause of this turnover, further investigation into gas reservoirs among nidal galaxies with 0.01 < sSFR < 0.1 is required. Additionally, the turnover of the specific SFR at high masses in nidal galaxies (sSFR > 0.01) appears more significant than previously recognized. While the influence of nuclear activity on the turning over of the sSFR-at-$M_{*}$ for nidal galaxies with LBT > 4Gyr remains modest, it could become more critical as the mass range is extended further. These findings support a model where star formation in high-mass nidal galaxies at late lookback times is regulated by central intense astronomical activity, consistent with the role of accreting supermassive black holes in capping both the sSFR-at-$M_{*}$ and the specific gas consumption rate-at-$M_{*}$ within this population. These central activity effects align with the "negative star formation law" observed in high-mass nidal galaxies at LBT > 4Gyr, mirroring the impact of black hole mass per unit $M_{*}$ on this relationship as reported by Behrooz et al.

This research sits at the intersection of computer science and linguistics, focusing on the challenge of cross-language sentiment analysis. Unlike previous studies that relied solely on unsupervised methods, our approach incorporates language models and deep learning within a framework that utilizes three datasets: two highly labeled ones for source languages and one unlabeled target language dataset. The system employs a multi-task learning strategy, integrating sentiment classification with back-translation. Notably, the source language datasets contain slipper-like expansions, which are excluded from the vocabulary used for the target language. Experimental results demonstrate that this configuration outperforms various baseline methods. The specific outcomes for each dataset are detailed in the sections following this introduction. Furthermore, we introduce a novel multi-task architecture where the number of tasks scales with the count of available languages. In this design, sentiment analysis serves as the primary task across all languages, while cross-lingual unsupervised representation learning functions as the secondary task. As illustrated in Figure 1, our multi-task learning framework processes two European languages, Arabic and Hebrew. The process begins with reading the Arabic and Hebrew datasets (D1 and D2), which are subsequently fed into neural networks to generate sentiment predictions (Y1 and Y2) and cross-lingual translations (T1 and T2). These steps are repeated for both languages, yielding two translated versions of the original datasets. Finally, these datasets undergo sentiment analysis to validate the sentiment of the cross-lingual translations. Multilayered neural networks are employed to generate sentiment predictions for both the source and target language datasets. Multi-head attention mechanisms are utilized to analyze sentences in the target language against those in the source languages, ultimately producing the final multi-task learning outcomes as shown in Figure 1. Multi-head neural networks also process the two source language datasets to determine the ultimate sentiment classification for the unlabeled target language dataset. This final classification is achieved through a softmax layer, which directs the L2 dataset toward either the positive or negative sentiment dataset. To accomplish this, two separate neural networks analyze the L2 dataset independently, as depicted in the same figure. The overall multi-task learning sentiment classification score for the L2 dataset was 0.82, confirming the effectiveness of our proposed architecture. Looking ahead, this work can be extended to additional languages, although such expansion would require a significant increase in computational resources. Furthermore, the current study is limited to analyzing textual data; future research should investigate whether this multi-task learning architecture can be successfully applied to modality-specific datasets, such as those involving images

During the thermal/bright state, the variable high-state spectrum exhibited a soft blackbody component and a hard power-law component, with the latter showing evidence of curvature. By tracking the innermost hot spot location via the type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPO), we determined the neutron star's mass ($M_{\rm NS}$) and radius ($R_{\rm NS}$) for both transients using a simple model. The derived parameters ($R_{\rm NS}=11.8^{+2.4}_{-1.8}$ km for AXT-1 and $10.9^{+2.0}_{-1.5}$ km for AXPer-1) suggest that these neutron stars possess low mass and large radius values. We discuss these findings in light of current neutron star mass-radius models. Furthermore, we analyzed the transient's variability properties and the spin up/down timescales to reconstruct the angular momentum accretion rate ($\dot{ }\Omega$). The results indicate that while the accretion rate ($\dot{M}$) correlated with the spin up/down timescales, the $\Omega\dot{M}$ product did not. This discrepancy suggests that either the angular momentum accretion rate ($\dot{ }\Omega$) or the mass accretion rate ($\dot{M}$) alone drives the spin timescales. Finally, we examined the neutron star's spin evolution, variability, and X-ray properties to propose potential formation channels for this ultra-fast rotating transient class. The surge in fake news, particularly during global crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, represents a significant threat to societal well-being. While existing detection methods primarily depend on linguistic characteristics of multimodal content, they struggle with unseen samples due to heavy reliance on data-specific features. This limitation becomes especially critical when applying models to new domains or languages, as gathering sufficient training data is often difficult or impossible. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a detection framework that effectively handles unseen multimodal samples by leveraging their underlying semantic attributes. In this study, we introduce a meta-learning approach that fuses image and text embeddings to address this challenge. Specifically, we propose a novel architecture based on Meta Neural Process Networks (MNPP) capable of detecting false news in unseen images and languages. Our framework utilizes an encoder to convert image and text samples into embeddings, which are subsequently processed by a Neural Process to generate predictions for unseen content via a network of artificial neurons. Validating our approach against two datasets—one covering unseen Italian articles and the other involving unseen images across multiple domains—we demonstrate that MNPP successfully identifies fake news in both scenarios. The results confirm that our framework effectively manages unseen images and languages, surpassing existing methods in these areas. Detailed descriptions of our architecture and findings are provided alongside the necessary equations and tables. An video overview of this work is available at https://youtu.be/0h6609676t0. Synthetic data serves as a crucial resource for developing algorithms capable of diagnosing brain injury (BI) from CT scans, particularly when real-labeled datasets are scarce. However, the efficacy of any synthetic approach is constrained by the final data distribution. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel method designed to generate biologically plausible CT images of brain injury. Building on a recent framework that combines variational auto-encoders (VAE) with a discriminative network for image reconstruction, our model adds a second discriminative network trained on biologically valid BI images. This creates a progressive system where two generative and two discriminative networks collaborate to produce clinically accurate brain injury synthesis. We evaluated the method using the public CT image dataset for brain injury (CAIR-BI). Significantly, our approach achieves state-of-the-art results without requiring data augmentation. To confirm that the generated images align with biological reality, we collected a balanced dataset of brain injury CT scans and healthy controls. We then trained a discriminative network on this set and applied it to evaluate both the original CAIR-BI data and our synthetic outputs. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of biological feasibility. Furthermore, a supporting dataset utilized for training and assessing this discriminative network on CAIR-BI, along with the corresponding code, is available at https://github.com/NehaGupta2000/VAE-VAE-VD. We anticipate that this work will prove valuable for developing biologically feasible brain injury synthetic data from CT images. Our proposed framework can also be adapted for other medical conditions involving specific patient cohorts, such as stroke and traumatic brain injury. Ultimately, this research holds significant potential for creating data-specific synthetic datasets for medical applications. Feature extraction serves as an effective strategy for addressing data scarcity in deep learning applications. Given the surge in unsupervised or weakly supervised datasets, the demand for robust and scalable feature extraction techniques is escalating. This paper introduces a novel contrastive learning-based method designed to unify various feature extraction approaches. While prior research has primarily focused on contrasting supervised methods like logistic regression, support vector machines, and deep networks among themselves, our proposed Unified Structure for Feature Extraction using Contrastive Learning (UniContrast) encompasses both supervised and unsupervised features. Within this framework, diverse explicit features are contrasted with implicit deep features. To achieve this, we incorporate a pre-trained deep network as a fixed encoder to generate implicit features from images. By leveraging contrastive learning, our system aligns the feature spaces of explicit and implicit features to ensure they carry equivalent semantic information. Extensive experiments conducted across three standard datasets—MNIST, EMNIST, and SVHN—demonstrate that UniContrast significantly outperforms existing feature extraction methods, yielding an average improvement of 3.36% on the EMNIST dataset and 2.56% on the SVHN dataset relative to previous state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rajivkumar2005/UniContrast.

We derive the Unruh-Wald volume law entropy for non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter black holes using the Unruh effect and Wald's "shades" framework. Our findings indicate that this entropy originates from the total acceleration horizon, comprising both the event and killing horizons. Furthermore, we address the third law of thermodynamics within the context of acceleration horizons. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Surface Area to Total Horizon Area (SATHA) ratio serves as a reliable indicator for the validity of the third law relative to the Event Horizon. Finally, we establish that the Unruh temperature of the Killing Horizon aligns with the Surface Gravity Temperature of the Event Horizon only when the Black Hole Charge remains below a specific threshold.

We present an experimental investigation into the entanglement structure of optical continuous variables using phase-space distributions, specifically optical tomograms. By constructing these distributions for two-mode squeezed thermal light, we were able to visualize changes in entanglement and the emergence of synchronization directly within the tomograms. Notably, we identified a non-local transition between mixed states and separable states in the Wigner distribution, manifested as a clear pattern in the optical tomograms at the specific point of change. At this same moment, the first-order correlation appeared as a valley in the tomogram, serving as a visible indicator of synchronization onset. Our findings demonstrate that entanglement alterations and synchronization onset can be clearly observed and measured in optical tomograms through both qualitative inspection and quantitative analysis. These results suggest that optical tomograms provide an effective framework for detecting shifts in entanglement and the beginning of synchronization. The methodology proposed here holds significant potential for other areas of quantum information science, including determining entanglement monotones and verifying quantum states. Generally, constructing a submodule lattice from multiplicity data remains theoretically significant but practically challenging, as the standard approach demands extensive computations and lacks scalability for specific multiplicity-free modules. This paper introduces novel methods to derive the lattice of submodules for an $\ell$-regular multiplicity-free module $M$ solely from its one-dimensional multiplicity function. Focusing on the third-symmetric power $M=sym^3(\ell)$, we apply these methods to explicitly construct its lattice, demonstrating that it corresponds to the lattice of submodules of $sym^3(\mathbb{C})$. Furthermore, we establish general criteria for determining when the submodule lattice of an $\ell$-regular multiplicity-free module $M$ aligns with that of $sym^3(\mathbb{C})$. These criteria are optimized specifically for $SL_3(\mathbb{C})$-regular $sym^3(\ell)$ modules where $\ell<0$. Numerical experiments suggest these guidelines remain effective even when $\ell\geq0$. The construction processes and the resulting lattice diagram for $sym^3(-7)$ under $SL_3(\mathbb{C})$ are presented as an appendix.

These definitions provide the foundation for analyzing the recurrent behaviors of various geometric objects, including submanifolds, within Euclidean and other ambient space forms.

This study investigates the acoustic emission (AE) spectrum of an adhesive tape being peeled at a constant speed. To capture the intermittent stick-slip dynamics, we employed a wavelet analysis to derive a local AE measure at specific frequency bands. This revealed a correlated double-step pattern in the local activity, corresponding to a two-stage local damping mechanism during detachment. Furthermore, a scaling relationship was identified within the local AE activity at individual frequency bands as a function of the stinging amplitude. This finding supports the applicability of Amplitude Scaling (AS) scaling—previously observed in earth tremors and seismic events— to the AE spectrum during adhesive detachment. Based on this AS scaling, we introduced a simple order parameter designed to distinguish between smooth and rough detachment phases. Notably, a critical slowing down in the peeling speed at a particular local AE activity level was observed, suggesting the emergence of a critical state within the system. These results suggest that this simple experimental setup serves as an effective model for studying earthquake phenomena. Consequently, both the correlated double-step pattern in the local AE activity at specific frequencies and the associated scaling relation may provide insights into pre-critical behaviors prior to seismic occurrences.

Menger developed the concept of a general metric space and subsequently explored how this idea could be applied to create an axiomatic framework for "angle spaces," ultimately linking them to metric spaces. Shortly after, he investigated whether an axiomatic definition of space could be formulated based on the proximity between points, concluding with two significant theorems. Around 1994, I attempted to systematize Menger's work by defining metric, point, and angle spaces, alongside their corresponding notions of isotony and invertibility. Geometric smoothing regularizers, such as Laplacian and convolutional smoothing, are essential for robust point cloud models that enhance resistance to noise and adversarial attacks. However, traditional regularizers fail to fully capture the distribution of point cloud data. This document introduces TPC-Net, a framework grounded in a novel smoothing technique called Transformation-Point Cloud (TPC) regularization. Unlike prior methods, TPC regularization processes point clouds by first applying individual transformations to each point before conducting convolutional smoothing on the resulting coordinates. This approach ensures that point clouds with identical semantic information retain consistent TPC representations, a capability absent in conventional regularization. We define uniqueness criteria for various point cloud representations under different transformations and demonstrate through theory and experiments that TPC regularization is the only method capable of satisfying these uniqueness criteria. Building on this, we establish a hierarchy of points, layers, and score functions within an adversarial robustness model to derive an exact closed-form solution for adversarial robustness against transformed W2P attacks, utilizing the TPC representation. Finally, we derive an upper-bound solution for robustness against general grid-based attacks (like L2 norm) in the coordinate space using TPC. Extensive experiments on standard point cloud datasets validate that the TPC-based point cloud models, particularly TPC-Net, achieve superior accuracy with higher certified adversarial robustness compared to state-of-the-art approaches. The open-source code for TPC-Net is accessible at https://github.com/haopeng3/TPC-Net. Notably, the source code for this document includes an implementation of the TPC-Netv2 framework.

Our goal is to equip a proof assistant with automated tools that enable it to verify proof scripts for certified libraries, libraries of certified libraries, and ultimately, certified programs. In this endeavor, we utilize the Coq proof assistant and developed a specialized version of the Z3 theorem prover called GeoCoq, which operates on a geometric reasoning framework rather than first-order logic with predicates. This geometric approach offers distinct advantages when assisting COQ in validating proofs for software certifications. Both the GeoCoq interpreter and the associated automated proof finding method are detailed in this paper and are available as open-source components of COQ. Our results demonstrate that this combination of tools can effectively verify programs and libraries that other automated reasoning systems, such as ICPS, RC1, and E-matching, have struggled to certify. Additionally, we observed significant byproducts regarding the extractable COFML code generated by COQ from these verified programs and libraries. This paper presents a novel approach to linking Serre weights with modular forms for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory. Unlike conventional methods, this approach does not rely on p-adic Hodge theory. Utilizing this new framework, we demonstrate a deterministic criterion for a Serre weight $\rho$ to be "重" (heavy) or "lightly heavy" based solely on its residual image. Applying this criterion, we establish that this property is hereditary under powers of the associated mod p Galois representation $\overline{\rho}_p$. Furthermore, we prove that every serre weight satisfying this heavyness condition is image heavy, thereby confirming Robert Langlands' heuristic prediction. As a byproduct of our framework, we also derive an explicit description of the action of complex conjugation on the (conjecturally存在的) crystalline-Lie algebra associated with $\rho$. In addition, we provide an explicit determination of the exact weight for the space of modular forms corresponding to any serre weight $\rho$ under our definition. Distinct from previous approaches, our formulation of "重" relies exclusively on the combinatorial characteristics of the congruence classes of primes $\l$ for which the Artin symbol $(\l/D)$ equals $-1$ and for which $\l$ has degree two over $\Q$ and is unramified, all considered modulo $p$. Consequently, this property is not inherently tied to the prime $q$ lying above 2 within the field $\Q_2(\zeta_q)$. This study presents an approach to exact damage shaping in self-sensing composite laminates via electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and genetic algorithms (GA). Although electrical impedance (EI) maps offer valuable insights into both the location and characteristics of damage, they do not directly enable the creation of specific damage geometries. By leveraging the strong correlation between applied load and EI, a genetic algorithm was developed to generate a stacking sequence for a [0/+45/-45/90]s composite that produces a target damage geometry as defined by the EI matrix. The resulting configuration, which achieves the desired geometry through localized impedance alterations, is termed a "fake damage geometry." Once formed, this geometry can be utilized for structural health monitoring (SHM) via electrical tomography; consequently, the method is overall referred to as exact damage shaping. The process involves two main stages: first, determining the stacking sequence to establish the fake damage geometry, and second, utilizing electrical tomography to visualize the actual geometry after formation. To facilitate this, a new shape optimization algorithm was introduced to minimize the mean squared error between the actual and target damage geometries. Validated with a [0/+45/-45/90]s laminate, the approach successfully achieved a star-shaped damage pattern with an accuracy of 94.2%. We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes manifest invariance under orthogonal transformations and isotropy, complemented by a specific geometric vector quantity. This approach enables the systematic construction of all Euclidean tensors, decomposing them into the preferred geometric vector and a set of invariant tensor coefficients. Consequently, this hierarchy of coefficients constitutes a viable model for the theory of Euclidean symmetries. Applying this system, we derive identities and formulas for vector products, vector powers, and spherical Bessel functions, demonstrating that these geometric elements can be treated as tensorial in nature. This works-in-progress establishes a foundation for a calculus of Euclidean shapes, potentially proving valuable across various domains of theoretical physics.

Iterative methods for matrix inversion, such as Newton--Alexandrov and Chebyshev--Halley algorithms, offer a compelling alternative to conventional direct inversion techniques like LU decomposition or Cayley--Hamilton based approaches, particularly for high-dimensional matrices on specialized hardware such as GPUs. This study focuses on optimizing these higher-order iterative methods and introduces a novel formulation capable of inverting large matrices on GPUs with logarithmic complexity relative to the dimension $N$. We validate these optimized algorithms against a Cayley--Hamilton based method, demonstrating significant speedups: the Newton--Alexandrov algorithm achieved a 2.7x improvement, while the Chebyshev--Halley algorithm reached a 4.2x improvement. Additionally, we present and assess the new higher-order method. Under specific conditions, this approach delivers substantial performance gains over both the Chebyshev--Halley algorithm and the Cayley--Hamilton based direct inversion technique. As a final contribution, we generalize this higher-order method to operate without prior knowledge of the convergence speed, proposing an optimal higher-order iterative algorithm. These higher-order iterative matrix inversion methods serve as a valuable alternative to Cayley--Hamilton based approaches for large-scale matrix inversion on GPUs, providing an efficient, robust, and accurate solution. This work is particularly relevant to electrical engineering, applied mathematics, and the fields of control and signal processing. Contextual linear bandits represent a significant area of research with extensive practical applications. In this landmark work, we investigate contextual linear bandits within a distributed setup, operating under the assumption that the underlying linearity dimension exceeds the actual linearity dimension. For deterministic contexts, we address both deterministic and stochastic scenarios regarding the context source in a fully distributed framework, where no point solutions are transferred from agents to the leader. In this environment, agents learn from local contexts drawn from an arbitrary source, while the leader selects the optimal action based on what the agents have learned. Prior to selection, the leader communicates a action description to the agents for execution. We demonstrate that the optimal action description length constitutes a fundamental limit for achievable regret. Specifically, for deterministic contexts, we establish a lower bound of $T^{2/3}$ and achieve it in the positive result for the stochastic scenario with a linearity dimension of two. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound of $T \cdot 2^{O(\dim{L})}$ for deterministic contexts and provide matching upper bounds for both deterministic and stochastic scenarios. These theoretical findings were implemented and validated using real-world data from a recommendation system at LinkedIn. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze learning in distributed contextual linear bandits where no actual learning occurs between the leader and agents, confirming that agents can be replaced by any other information processing entity, such as in a multi-armed bandit context. Additionally, these results hold true for fully Bayesian settings. Crucially, all our outcomes apply regardless of how the context source is distributed among agents in the distributed scenario. We conclude by outlining several open problems in this domain. The core methodologies developed here may find broader applications in various fields. Our implementations of these methods were utilized to derive several novel results for recommendation systems and were experimentally verified using real-world data from LinkedIn.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) represents a theoretical mechanism capable of generating rapid gas rotation in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. However, this instability operates within a parameter range that is closely linked to the thermal profile, which in turn depends heavily on dust evolution. Consequently, the viability of the VSI amidst ongoing dust evolution remains uncertain. This study conducts a comprehensive investigation into how dust evolution influences the VSI in the outer regions of minimal solar nebulae and Disc Initial Conditions (DIC-ICs). Our analysis reveals that dust growth and settling thermally stabilize the vertical shear; furthermore, larger grains and greater midplane temperatures result in enhanced stability. Based on this finding, we propose that the effectiveness of VSI turbulence accelerates dust growth and setting, creating a feedback loop. Ultimately, within the outer regions of both the minimal solar nebula and DIC-ICs, dust growth and settling push the vertical shear beyond its instability threshold, thereby suppressing VSI turbulence. These conclusions hold true even when opacity variations caused by dust evolution are taken into account. Finally, we suggest that future research should explore the impact of other instability-driven turbulence, such as the gravitational instability, on the outer regions of protoplanetary disks in light of dust evolution. This study examines a Laplacian comparison theorem derived from a recent work by Bakry and Qian (B&Q), alongside another comparison result established by the first author (Wang). We demonstrate that the Liouville theorem previously proven by Wang does not necessarily follow from the concave Liouville theorem introduced by Anderson in 2000. Furthermore, leveraging the Laplacian comparison provided by B&Q, we prove a new Liouville theorem under the assumption of uniformly bounded scalar curvature. As a consequence, we show that an ancient solution to the Ricci flow satisfying certain curvature constraints must be shrinking. This final result aligns with the theorem recently presented by Bakry and Qian. Additionally, we establish a mean convexity theorem based on the Liouville principles of both the first author and B&Q. Finally, we provide a proof for an eigenvalue theorem concerning gradient shrinking Ricci shrinkers, utilizing the Liouville results from the first author and Anderson. We conclude with an discussion regarding a related problem. It is important to note that this manuscript complements the work of the first author (Wang) described above. The rise of outsourced neural network training has introduced significant security concerns, as systems have become vulnerable to sophisticated backdoor attacks. Recently, authors of \cite{global} demonstrated that image classification models can be poisoned using a "dynamic backdoor" with global mean pooling, requiring camouflage additions and adding images globally rather than as individual samples. This approach is effective only when the attacker has access to the training pipeline but lacks knowledge of the underlying architecture or loss function. In this work, we show that dynamic backdoors can be implemented with various camouflage strategies, often reducing the needed additive pixels by up to 75%. We experiment with different global activation functions, camouflage types, and data additions. Our findings indicate that sine transformations combined with pixelwise camouflage yield the most effective results. Conversely, simple mean pooling is highly susceptible to noise, and constant convolutional layers offer no advantage over global fully connected layers. These experiments highlight the significance of data characteristics—such as mean, variance, and higher-order statistics—over specific features like pixel values or convolutional kernels. We conclude by discussing the practical implications of these results for real-world scenarios. The source for this system is available at: https://github.com/AliAlrshidi/GlobalBackdoor. Our code can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10134020.

This work addresses the challenge of federated learning (FL) under data distribution heterogeneity, where global data follows a non-i.i.d. distribution. Unlike conventional methods that rely on gradient-based optimization, we propose Stroll-for-Learning (Stroll), a random walk (RW)-based algorithm specifically designed for language models. By leveraging the ability of RW algorithms to identify and revisit high-probability events, Stroll optimizes local model parameters by selecting data points with higher probability distributions for training. These points are then shared to update the global model. Evaluation on English and Mandarin cross-lingual natural language inference (XLI) datasets—specifically MultiRC and XNLI—shows that Stroll outperforms existing FL approaches. Furthermore, results across various NLP tasks indicate that this method is universally effective. As a consequence, Stroll offers a practical solution for language models facing data distribution heterogeneity, potentially becoming essential for real-world deployments, such as in the telecommunications sector. Extensive experiments confirm that Stroll surpasses current state-of-the-art random walk algorithms in both recommendation systems and cross-lingual NLP tasks. Additional details, source code, and a video demonstration are available at https://github.com/yzh2019/Stroll-for-Learning and https://youtube.com/watch?v=VPyWa66rd38. We anticipate that this algorithm will have significant impact in both academic research and industrial applications.

This paper introduces a new regularization approach for semi-supervised medical image segmentation that leverages distribution matching. By utilizing a simple "one-hot" consistency penalty, the method encourages the network to generate one-hot encoded predictions on unlabeled data, which are then one-hot decoded and compared against continuous predictions on the same data. This creates a form of distribution matching between supervised and unsupervised batches. The approach requires no additional constraints, such as adversarial games, metric learning, or auxiliary tasks, and performs effectively in a end-to-end manner without needing manual tuning of a "temperature" parameter. Extensive evaluations on three public medical image segmentation datasets demonstrate that this method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/XUSong/Awkdward_One_Hot_Consistency. We gratefully acknowledge the RAISE project (grant no. 824094) for their financial support.

Although the integration of 5G and IoT has generated massive data volumes in Internet of Vehicles (IoV) environments, centralizing this data for analysis or training creates significant privacy risks and high communication overhead. Consequently, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for IoV data processing. Meanwhile, Blockchain offers robust security and management capabilities through features like decentralized storage, immutability, and traceability. When combined with FL, Blockchain can enhance security, ensure accountability, optimize resource allocation, and improve overall system performance within IoV contexts. This review examines the application of Blockchain-empowered FL frameworks for IoV, highlighting their key characteristics, advantages, and potential directions for development. Furthermore, it addresses critical challenges concerning security, privacy, and system performance in these frameworks. Finally, the review discusses emerging trends in Blockchain-empowered FL for IoV and offers suggestions for future research. The proposed security model for these frameworks is characterized by access control, authentication, encryption, logging, and anomaly detection. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks extensively utilized for sequence analysis and identification tasks, such as video identification. However, their substantial computational demands lead to high energy consumption and limited suitability for real-time video identification. To address this issue and enhance the energy efficiency of LSTMs in video identification scenarios, this study introduces an innovative hardware- and algorithm-co-designed approach based on the Hierarchical Tucker (HT) decomposition. Specifically, an algorithmic co-design utilizing HT decomposition is proposed to optimize LSTM networks, while a corresponding hardware co-design was developed to implement the resulting hierarchical Tucker-LSTM (HT-LSTM) structure. These designs aim to maximize energy efficiency by leveraging the low-rank characteristics of LSTMs through HT decomposition for algorithmic optimization and by exploiting parallel computation capabilities in the hardware implementation. Validation via both real-world video data and synthesized sequences demonstrates that the proposedHT-LSTM architecture achieves significant energy efficiency gains compared to conventional LSTMs. Furthermore, the algorithmic and hardware co-design strategies exhibit mutual benefits; the HT-LSTM structure facilitates hardware design optimizations, while specific hardware constraints guided further algorithmic refinements. Ultimately, this work delivers a comprehensive end-to-end solution encompassing data processing, network algorithmic design, and hardware implementation for real-time video identification. The findings offer valuable insights and a practical framework for the algorithmic and hardware co-design of energy-efficient LSTMs, applicable to various sequence identification scenarios. A summary of this end-to-end approach using a real-time video recognition scenario is provided in Table 1, which highlights the coordination between video data, the HT-LSTM algorithm, and the underlying hardware architecture. The actual hardware prototype was constructed using an FPGA board equipped with an Xilinx KV260 chip featuring a Vivado™ environment. These experiments were conducted on a workstation running Windows 10 with 32GB of RAM and an NVIDIA GTX 2080 Ti GPU, utilizing PyTorch version 1.8.1 for the LSTM/HT-LSTM development and MATLAB R2020a for HT decomposition calculations. This study explores the connection between the primality of $n$ and the primality of $x+n$ when $x$ is a product of two integers around the magnitude of $n$. Leveraging this concept, we introduce a novel prime characterization that requires no prior knowledge of the Euclidean algorithm or Euclid-Mulliner "back-smoothing" technique. Consequently, this new characterization offers a straightforward proof of Euclid's Mulliner's Mulliner-Euclid lemma (referred to as the Mulliner-Euclid lemma), which in turn establishes Euclid's Mulliner-Mulliner-Euclid lemma (or Mulliner- lemma), ultimately yielding a fresh proof of Bertrand's postulate. Additionally, we define a revised Euclid-Mulliner sieve, distinct from both the Eratosthenes sieve and the Atkin sieve. By combining this sieve with the prime characterization, we demonstrate that any integer $n$ greater than a specific constant $C$ is prime if and only if the function $f(x)=x^2+n}$ composed with itself $k$ times ($k\geq 1$), followed by the linear transformation $g(x)=x-c$ (where $c$ is that constant), yields a sequence of values that factorize via the Mulliner-Euclid "back-smoothing" method into two components of nearly identical size. Finally, we prove that every integer $n$ exceeding this constant $C$ is prime precisely when such a factorization pattern can be achieved through repeated squaring-addition ($x^2+n$) and Mulliner-Euclid "back-smoothing" into two factors of comparable magnitude. This result yields an innovative prime-number theorem, an innovative Mulliner-Euclid lemma, and a new proof of Bertrand's postulate, all derived via the Mulliner-Euclid sieve, the new prime characterization, and the third author's "two-cuts" technique. We conclude by defining a hierarchy of functions based on the $k$-fold iteration of the "squared-addition" function $x^2+n$ and the Euclid-Mulliner sieve, and presenting a new lemma regarding this structure.

This paper examines the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation defined on the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^d$ ($d\geq 1$), subject to a nonlocal boundary condition. We demonstrate that the solution may experience a "explosion" phenomenon, characterized by a blow-up in norm, when the initial data possesses a specific concentration. This result holds true for both focusing and defocusing scenarios, provided the nonlinearity is in the energy-critical category. To achieve this, we introduce a new "mass-losing" solution to the Schr\"odinger equation on the exterior of the obstacle and utilize a unique continuation argument tailored for this geometric setting. Additionally, we establish global existence for data satisfying certain novel inequalities. These findings represent the first report on explosion phenomena arising from nonlocal boundary conditions in a geometric domain within the context of NLS. Distinct from previous work, our proof does not rely on the compactness of the underlying domain.

This work introduces a non-standard approach to algebraic geometry, utilizing semi-parametric local constructions over commutative, finitely produced Q-algebras. These methods enable the derivation of positive-characteristic results from characteristic-zero assumptions, thereby yielding local variety overlogs in positive characteristic from failing in such contexts. The authors apply these techniques to prove the existence of local Chevalley-Serre-Néron expansions for varieties over Poincaré local rings of characteristic p > 0, demonstrating that every variety defined over a finitely produced Q-algebra (specifically, the integer algebra Z/(n)) admits such an expansion. Additionally, they establish analogous results for Davis-Robinson-Chabir expansions. Central to this research is a new method for transferring varieties between different characteristics, which they term the "lift-swim" technique.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors serving as a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors offer significant advantages over p-values in certain aspects, they remain highly sensitive to specific data characteristics and the structural details of the calculations themselves. This collection of essays was inspired by the presentation, "Workflow Strategies for the Robust Use of Bayes Factors," by Joseph Asparouchiov and Brad St. Amant at the XXII Symposium on Cognitive Science in Leipzig. The central goal of this work is to identify practical steps for optimizing the application of Bayes factors when comparing Bayesian estimations across diverse datasets. These strategies are designed to mitigate the influences of data-related factors that can skew Bayes factor calculations, providing a more reliable framework for analysis. The resulting approaches yield a refined, nuanced metric for evaluating cognitive theories against empirical evidence, which may prove more advantageous than the traditional method of treating Bayes factors as a simple decision rule. Discourse markers, such as $\it therefore$ and $\it in\ contrast$, are words that signal specific semantic relationships between clauses. Although recent studies have employed machine learning techniques to classify these relationships based on the marker used, such approaches require extensive manually labeled training data. Furthermore, neither machine learning nor rule-based solutions offer guaranteed correct classifications for unseen sentences. This work presents an automatic method to validate the semantic appropriateness of discourse markers in specific sentences using a discourse representation theory-based classifier. The dataset for this task was manually created and is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkshri/DiscSense}. Ultimately, this dataset and the associated classifier serve as a valuable resource for linguistic research and the development of natural language understanding systems. We conclude by highlighting potential applications of this dataset and classifier. The underlying open-source code is available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkshri/DiscSense}. This paper introduces a unified family of deformations that generalize both the Jordanian and Drinfel'd twist solutions within the drinfel'd double cohomology. We demonstrate that this family precisely corresponds to the conjugation of Drinfel'd twists by a solution to the homomorphism equation, thereby extending a result originally established for Jordanian twists. Furthermore, we provide a explicit construction of the associated COHOMOMORPHION equation. Finally, we apply this generalized twisting framework to the KPV Lax operator, deriving a unified set of deformed Lax operators. These results suggest that a similar conjugation relationship between regular quantum group Lax operators and deformed Lax operators constructed from a generalized Drinfel'd twist exists, mirroring the known connection between the AdS Lax operator and its $PSU(2,2|4)$ counterpart, as opposed to the relationship between AdS and Jordanian Lax operators. Additionally, we sketch how this generalized twisting approach can be extended to unify the deformation of action functionals previously developed by JO, AK, and JOBJ.

We introduce the concept of multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics to create a monitoring telescope capable of performing X-ray imaging over a $50^{\circ}$ field of view using a compact 2-m diameter instrument. This design utilizes a matrix of small lobster-eye modules, each with a $3^{\circ}$ field of view, which direct X-rays onto a multiplexing mechanism that folds the optical path to fit the modules onto a flat detector plane. Several configurations for this multiplexing system are evaluated, with a diffractive grating selected as the most effective solution. Simulations are employed to assess the overall instrument performance across these different designs. Additionally, the feasibility of constructing such a telescope using existing lobster-eye technology is discussed.

We present a novel approach to examine how the cosmic velocity field influences the dark matter halo mass function within an dark energy–dominated universe. Leveraging N-body simulations, we employed a deep learning framework to recreate the halo mass function by integrating the standard Poissonian model. Our results indicate that this conventional model fails to accurately predict the dark matter halo mass function when significant non-Gaussianity arises from rapid, high-amplitude velocity fluctuations, as seen in UNIVARIANT simulations. Consequently, a new model incorporating a "cosmic speed field" is required. We trained a neural network to determine this field and derive an effective "cosmic speed overdensity" $\delta_{s}$. Our findings reveal a strong correlation between $\delta_{s}$ and the halo mass function, enabling a straightforward calculation of the function via the speed field alone. Furthermore, we derived an analytical expression for $\delta_{s}$ based on both line-of-sight and 3D velocity fluctuations, which successfully reproduces the dark matter halo mass function across different cosmological volumes and redshifts when combined with the neural network model. Ultimately, this study provides a practical method for directly observing the impact of velocity fluctuations on structure formation through future astronomical data, such as redshift surveys and redshift-space power spectra. Specifically, such data can be used to derive the anisotropic "cosmic speed overdensity" and subsequently extract the amplitude of velocity fluctuations. Additionally, by analyzing the amplitude of fluctuations in the line-of-sight and 3D directions, we can constrain the growth rate $f$ and the distortion parameter $\beta$, ultimately determining the velocity fluctuation amplitude and assessing the validity of the UNIVARIANT simulation's velocity spectrum.

Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we demonstrate a local probe capable of measuring weak magnetic fields up to 10 $\mu$T with a resolution of 24 fT per 100 s. The approach involves subjecting an atomic interferometer to a previously undetected local field generated by a superconducting Meissner effect. This field falls within the instrument's detection range, enabling precision measurement. Consequently, the ultimate sensitivity is determined by the noise floor of the atomic interferometer when detecting fields weaker than the local maximum ($B_{max} \approx 50$ nT). We validate this method in a laboratory setting and confirm its effectiveness with a commercially available 3D superconductor. Additionally, we establish the feasibility of this technique for magnetometry on airborne and satellite platforms. Such applications could offer novel insights into geomagnetism and assist in identifying magnetic anomalies linked to mineral exploration or geological faults. Finally, this work represents the first demonstration of magnetometry leveraging the Meissner effect. The detailed description of this method will be published in Phys. Rev. Lett. under the title: Sensitive detection of local magnetic field variations with atomic interferometry via the superconducting Meissner effect. (c) 2020 American Physical Society. We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to calculate the electronic states of magnetic adatoms and clusters resting on metallic surfaces, specifically targeting the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states emerging from local resonant levels within the surface states of the substrate. Within the self-consistent tight-binding framework, we examine the YSR states of an Mn adatom and Mn_n (n=2,3,4) clusters on the Nb(110) surface. Our calculated spin-resolved local density of states for these systems aligns well with recent experimental data obtained via scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Specifically, the calculated Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state for the Mn adatom matches the experimental observations, confirming the validity of our theoretical approach.

This research presents a framework for classifying the BST32,000 dataset, which consists of 109,039 dermoscopic images. The dataset contains seven categories: benign lesion (BL), melanoma in situ (MS), lateral spreading melanoma (LM), nodular melanoma (NM), superficial spreading melanoma (SSM), unknown (UNK), and malignant melanoma (MM), representing a multi-class scenario. To achieve this, we developed a three-step approach. First, an autoencoder (AE) was trained on the BL and MS images to reconstruct and segment them individually from the remaining five categories. Second, the remaining categories were divided into two groups: melanoma (MS, LM, NM, SSM, MM) and non-melanoma (BL), which were classified separately using a convolutional neural network (CNN). Finally, the AE outputs for both categories were analyzed to identify and separate the unknown (UNK) class. Notably, this process occurred without labeling the UNK samples during training. To determine the UNK category, we examined the AE reconstruction errors of the melanoma and non-melanoma groups; samples with high error rates were identified as UNK based on their visual characteristics. Validating this method, the non-melanoma category (including BL and UNK) was correctly segmented with 99.4% accuracy, and the melanoma group (MS, LM, NM, SSM, MM) was accurately classified with 96.1% accuracy. Furthermore, the identified UNK samples were correctly labeled with 98% precision. To highlight the segmentation of all seven classes, we introduced a visualization technique that combines entropy with a heat map. The segmentation of melanoma, non-melanoma, and UNK samples is distinctly visible in the heat map through variations in entropy values. Ultimately, the overall classification accuracy for all seven categories reached 95.9%. The detailed classification report and the architectural diagram of the proposed model are available at the following URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167864X1930330X?via%3Dihub. In summary, this study provides a practical solution for analyzing the BST32,000 dataset and offers a scalable framework applicable to other dermoscopic datasets.

Because of the forward-peaked exchange of electroweak bosons, lepton-lepton collisions at center-of-mass energies below a few TeV can be efficiently described using the Equivalent Vector Boson Approximation (EVA). This paper introduces an "efficient" version of the EVA specifically for high-energy muon-lepton scattering. We demonstrate that, within the EVA framework, the polarization-dependent behavior of electroweak bosons can be effectively managed by incorporating Regge behaviors and leading-power mass terms. Furthermore, we provide a detailed comparison of the EVA and rigorous unitary gauge approaches across various muon-lepton center-of-mass energies. Under the EVA, computational efficiencies reach approximately 90.6% for $\mu^-e^-$ and 99.9% for $\mu^-{\nu}_\mu$ scattering at 20 TeV. We also present optimized algorithms for generating leading-order weak and electroweak amplitudes in the EVA using both EPAStar and MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. These tools enable the systematic exploration of physically viable EVA processes at high-energy lepton colliders, such as the muon collider ($\mu^+\mu^-$), through advanced parton shower and matrix element matching procedures. Ultimately, this study highlights the practical utility of the efficient EVA for calculating electroweak processes in high-energy muon collisions. Supporting equations (1)-(90) and 9 figures are included.

This research demonstrates the inverse challenge of reconstructing a boundary shape to eliminate an on-shell acoustic mode in a structural-acoustic system. Initially, the feasibility of this inversion is shown through a numerical simulation involving a two-dimensional plate coupled with an acoustic cavity. Subsequently, the actual boundary shape reconstruction is achieved experimentally using a rectangular plate and an enclosed acoustic domain. The successful inversion confirms that the shape modification effectively prevented the target acoustic mode from resonating. These findings validate the viability of designing boundary or interface shapes to modify shape-geometric characteristics and suppress specific acoustic modes within an enclosed volume, offering valuable insights for applications in noise control, vibration isolation, and sonar. Accordingly, this work constitutes an inverse problem addressed within the field of structural-acoustic interaction. The reconstruction of boundary shape serves as a final example of active control strategies, complementing prior discussions on material and parameter variations. Further details regarding this progression of concepts are outlined in the introduction and are not repeated here. We introduce the simplest variant of scoto-seesaw Model 2, featuring the minimal field content necessary for fermion masses to arise via the mechanism. Due to this constrained simplicity, quantum corrections to the Higgs mass significantly enhance its stability, permitting a vacuum stability mass scale of approximately $100$ PeV and a light Higgs mass of $125$ GeV. Within this narrow parameter space, neutrino oscillation data and the specific dynamics of early universe neutrino oscillations tightly constrain the model's predictions. We determine that the lightest neutral dark matter candidate, a scalar neutrino, possesses a mass of $48.1^{+3.8}_{-4.0}$ MeV to satisfy neutrino oscillation constraints, while the smallest active-neutrino mass, $m_1 = 7.6^{+0.5}_{-0.4}$ mE, is fixed by oscillation parameters and the see-saw scale. We examine the dark matter coannihilation cross section, neutrinoless double beta decay, electric dipole moments of neutrons and neutral mesons, and other phenomena relevant to future experiments and fixed-target experiments like SHiP. Furthermore, we analyze the thermal history of the early universe, highlighting several interesting non-thermal processes. Our results indicate that neutrinoless majorana beta decay offers the most promising new physics signature. Finally, we find that stable neutral dark matter with a mass precisely equal to $48.1$ MeV can be produced in significant quantities by the CMORSE mechanism at the MRX experiment.
